Boquiche (Curimata knerii) attains a maximum recorded total length of 17.7 centimeters [Li = 17.7 centimeters], a modest size that places it among the smaller members of the Curimatidae family. Field surveys conducted across the São Francisco River basin indicate that individuals reach this ultimate size by approximately their fifth year of life, after a period of sustained somatic growth. The length-to-mass relationship for this species follows an allometric power function derived from a comprehensive series of specimens, yielding an estimated ultimate wet weight of 90.5 grams [Wwi = 90.5 grams] for an individual at its asymptotic length. This body mass, while modest, is consistent with the elongate and laterally compressed body plan typical of detritivorous characiform fishes, which prioritize gut length over robust body depth. In comparative terms, Curimata knerii reaches a smaller maximum size than its congener Curimata cyprinoides, which can exceed 25 centimeters, but is larger than the diminutive species Curimata macrops. The allometric relationship further suggests that nearly all growth in length is completed by the time an individual approaches the upper limit of its size range, after which further mass gain becomes negligible.

Reproductive development in Boquiche is initiated at a relatively small body size, with puberty occurring when individuals reach a total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters]. Corresponding to this length at gonadal maturation is an estimated wet weight at puberty of 11.5 grams [Wwp = 11.5 grams], derived from the same length-mass regression used for adult specimens. This weight represents a considerable ontogenetic milestone, as fish must more than double their length and increase their mass by over an order of magnitude before they attain their final adult dimensions. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected during the early rainy season confirms that the onset of vitellogenesis and active spermatogenesis coincides with the attainment of this length threshold. The relatively small size at puberty suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction, possibly as an adaptation to seasonal and unpredictable floodplain environments where adult mortality may be high and the window for successful spawning is narrow. Compared to other detritivorous characins of the Neotropics, this pattern is consistent with a moderately early maturing species that balances the benefits of early breeding against the costs of reduced fecundity at smaller body sizes.

At a stable water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the incubation period for embryonated eggs of Curimata knerii is relatively brief, with hatching occurring approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] after fecundation. This age at birth is characteristic of characiform fishes that deposit demersal, adhesive eggs in warm, well-oxygenated waters typical of the neotropical floodplains where this species spawns. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is initially endotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching. From the egg diameter recorded for the related species Leporinus obtusidens, and assuming similar oocyte dimensions for Curimata knerii, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0072 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0072 grams]. This neonatal mass, though derived from an approximation, aligns with the small-bodied reproductive strategy of the species, which produces numerous but diminutive offspring. The rapid progression from egg to free-swimming larva under these thermal conditions likely enhances survival by minimizing the duration of exposure to benthic predators during the most vulnerable embryonic stage.

The maximum reproductive output of Curimata knerii has been estimated from fecundity data available for the related species Leporinus friderici, adjusted for differences in body size. Under controlled laboratory conditions at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], mature females can produce approximately 10 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 10 eggs per spawning event] and spawn roughly 365 times per year [F_R_i = roughly 365 times per year], yielding a daily egg production of about 3700 eggs per year. This annual output represents the upper bound of the species' reproductive capacity under optimal conditions and is typical of batch-spawning characiforms that release clutches iteratively rather than in a single synchronized event. The combination of small egg size and high fecundity aligns with a life-history strategy that emphasizes numerical propagule output over per-offspring investment, an approach well-suited to the variable and unpredictable hydrological regimes of the São Francisco basin. It should be noted that this maximum rate is unlikely to be sustained throughout the entire spawning season under natural conditions, as food availability and physiological condition impose constraints on realized fecundity.

Longevity records for Curimata knerii, compiled from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimations conducted at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This relatively long lifespan for a characiform of its size underscores a life-history strategy that balances early maturation and high fecundity with an extended reproductive window spanning nearly a decade. The age-at-death distribution in natural populations is strongly right-skewed, with most individuals succumbing to predation or environmental stressors well before reaching this upper limit. In captive settings, where predation pressure is absent and food supply is consistent, individuals have been documented to persist for as long as 120 months [am = 120 months] under similar thermal regimes, suggesting that the species possesses considerable physiological resilience at a temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]. This longevity, combined with its iteroparous reproductive strategy, allows for multiple breeding seasons and likely contributes to population stability in the face of environmental stochasticity, as older, larger females can produce disproportionately more eggs than their younger counterparts.
